summary: Specifies a "simple mode" for sending facsimile data using Internet mail, using standard protocols and file formats such as MIME and TIFF. It can send to Internet-aware fax devices and other mail recipients, and extensions are to follow.

plainLanguage.summary: It lets you send a fax as a normal email with the page as a picture attached, so ordinary email systems can carry faxes.

questions: how to send a fax by email
what image format does internet fax use
subtitle: How to send a fax as an ordinary email with a TIFF image attached, and how gateways bridge to phone-line fax machines.

tldr.problem: Fax machines and Internet mail were separate worlds, and people wanted to send a fax to email users, network printers and phone-line fax machines without special new services.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a profile of Internet mail: the page images travel as minimum-set TIFF for Facsimile files in MIME messages over normal mail transport, with offramp gateways forwarding to G3Fax devices.
tldr.outcome: It is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2305 with no technical changes, and it sets a baseline that later extensions were to build on.

facts.label: Image format
facts.value: Minimum set TIFF for Facsimile (S profile)

facts.label: Multi-page documents
facts.value: SHOULD be one multi-page TIFF file

today: RFC 3965 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2305; the revision made no technical changes. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Faxes as a Profile of Internet Mail
sections.content:
RFC 3965 specifies a simple mode of facsimile: message-based fax communication over the Internet that uses standard protocols and file formats such as TCP/IP, Internet mail, MIME and TIFF for Facsimile. It describes a minimum set of capabilities, taking into account typical fax devices and PCs that can generate fax data.

Rather than inventing a separate fax-over-the-Internet service, the RFC defines a profile of Internet mail. The stated reason is interworking: existing email users should be able to send ordinary messages to lists that include fax recipients, and recipients should be able to reply and keep the fax recipients on the thread, with existing email software working without modification.

A fax device that uses T.4 over the general switched telephone network (GSTN) is a G3Fax device. An IFax device is an Internet-accessible device that can send, receive or forward Internet faxes.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of building a whole new fax network, the authors teach regular email to carry faxes. That way anyone with email can talk to fax machines.

sections.title: Relays, Gateways and Mailbox Protocols
sections.content:
Data transfer MAY use standard Internet mail transfer. Addresses MUST conform to the RFC 821 addr-spec and RFC 822 mailbox standards.

A gateway translates between Internet mail and T.4/GSTN fax. An onramp goes from fax to Internet mail; an offramp goes from Internet mail to fax. Onramp behavior is out of scope; the RFC covers the mail-side addressing, confirmation and failure notification of offramps.

A gateway that acts as a mail transfer agent for many users SHOULD use SMTP. A gateway that acts as a mail user agent for a single recipient MAY use a mailbox access protocol such as POP. An offramp that relays based on addressing must use the addresses in the MTA envelope, not those in the message content headers.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway is a doorway between email and the phone-line fax world. An offramp is the door that lets an email out to a fax machine.

sections.title: Message Headers, MIME and Content
sections.content:
IFax devices MUST comply with RFC 2822 and RFC 1123 for headers. A message SHOULD include Message-ID and MUST include all required fields such as DATE and FROM. They MUST also comply with MIME, except for the exceptions listed in Appendix A.

The image data is based on the minimum set of TIFF for Facsimile, also called the S profile, carried in a MIME object with the image/TIFF sub-type.

A multi-page document SHOULD be sent as a single multi-page TIFF file, though recipients MUST process multipart/mixed containing several TIFF files. If any part fails to process, the entire message is treated as failing.
sections.plainLanguage: The fax pages are packed into one picture file and attached to the email. Several pages go in one file if possible.

sections.title: Delivery and Processing Failures
sections.content:
If a relay fails, the sending relay MUST generate a failure message, which SHOULD be in the format of a delivery status notification (DSN). Internet mail sent over SMTP MUST carry a MAIL FROM address suitable for return notices.

IFax devices with limited capabilities may be unable to process a message. The RFC wants such a message not to vanish silently, but notice MAY be given in any appropriate fashion and the exact handling is a local matter.
sections.plainLanguage: If a fax cannot be delivered or a simple device cannot read it, somebody should be told, like a returned letter.

sections.title: Addressing Email and Fax Recipients
sections.content:
Ordinary email recipients use standard Internet mail addresses with no extra constraints. G3Fax devices are reached through an offramp gateway, which performs any authorized telephone dial-up.

When a G3Fax device is identified by a telephone number, the whole address, including the number and the offramp host, MUST be inside standard mail transport fields such as RCPT TO and MAIL FROM. The local part of an address is interpreted only by the MTA named in the domain. The telephone number format SHOULD conform to RFC 3191 and RFC 3192, and other formats MUST be syntactically distinct from those.
sections.plainLanguage: To reach a fax machine you write its phone number into the email address, along with the name of the gateway that will dial it.

sections.title: The Image File Format
sections.content:
Sending IFax devices MUST be able to write minimum set TIFF files, and receiving devices MUST be able to read them. These follow the S profile rules in TIFF for Facsimile.

A sender SHOULD NOT use TIFF fields and values beyond the minimum subset unless it knows the recipient supports them. How to learn a recipient's capabilities is beyond the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone agrees on one simple kind of picture file so any sender and receiver can understand each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Any security should be part of the existing Internet security infrastructure rather than a new mechanism. The RFC lists threats that come from joining fax with mail: spoofed senders, resources consumed by dialout, disclosure of GSTN authorization information such as calling card numbers, sender accountability, message disclosure, non-private mailboxes receiving bounces, and traffic analysis.

Offramp gateways SHOULD be able to authorize senders, because an outdial can cost real money and unsolicited bulk email that causes an outdial is undesirable. Offramps SHOULD give fax recipients contact information and enough data to trace the originator. The RFC points to channel security (IPSec and TLS) and object security (PGP-MIME and S/MIME) for information.
sections.plainLanguage: Because an email can make a gateway place a phone call that costs money, gateways should check who is asking. Secret numbers should not be printed on the fax page.

sections.title: Exceptions to MIME
sections.content: Appendix A allows three exceptions. IFax senders are not required to be able to send text/plain messages, although recipients are required to accept and process them. Recipients are not required to offer to put results in a file. Recipients MAY directly print or fax a received message rather than display it.
sections.plainLanguage: Because some devices are just printers, they get a few small passes from the usual email rules, such as printing a message instead of showing it on a screen.
